title: Browser DevTools and the Console
sub: Open the developer tools in Safari and Chrome, drive any page from the Console, read the Network waterfall, inspect storage, and debug JavaScript with breakpoints instead of guesses
goals: Open Web Inspector in Safari and DevTools in Chrome, and pick the panel that answers your question
Use the Console API (format specifiers, table, group, count, assert, time) and the console utilities ($0, $$, $x, copy, inspect)
Scrape and change a live page from the Console and turn the result into JSON for Terminal
Read a request in the Network pane, from status and headers to timing phases, and replay it with fetch or curl
Debug a script with line, conditional and DOM breakpoints, stepping, Scope and the call stack
Inspect and edit localStorage, sessionStorage and cookies, and know what HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite protect

blocks.text: Every browser ships a full development environment, hidden one shortcut away. In this chapter you will open it in Safari and Chrome, learn what each panel is for, and use it the way professionals do: query and scrape a router's status page from the Console, find out which CSS rule paints a button, watch a retry against a flaky API in the Network pane, copy a request as a `curl` command for Terminal, pause a buggy script on the exact line that fails, and edit what a site stores about you. The skill underneath all of it is the same as in [Errors and debugging](#py-errors): stop guessing, observe the program while it runs, and change one thing at a time.

The `devtools` practice pages and playgrounds in this chapter have a drawer with **Console**, **Elements**, **Network** and **Storage**, wired to the practice server at `http://lab.local`. Everything else (the Sources debugger, Performance, Lighthouse) needs a real browser, so keep a Terminal tab ready to serve `~/lab/web` with `python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1`, as in [How the Web Works](#web-intro).
Opening the tools on your Mac

**Chrome** has DevTools switched on out of the box. **Safari** hides its Web Inspector until you enable it once: Safari > Settings… (⌘,) > Advanced > tick **Show features for web developers**. A **Develop** menu appears in the menu bar. Versions before Safari 17 call the same checkbox "Show Develop menu in menu bar".

head: Action
Chrome
Safari (developer features on)
rows: Open the tools on the last-used panel
Pick an element by clicking it in the page

blocks.text: The Safari shortcuts are the ones Apple and WebKit document for current Safari (27); the menu items name the same commands if you prefer the mouse. The tools dock to the bottom or side of the window or float in their own window (Chrome: the ⋮ menu > Dock side; Safari: the buttons at the top left of the inspector). Docked to the right suits wide screens; undocked suits a second display.

DevTools belongs to the tab it was opened from and closes with it. If you open a page in a new tab, open DevTools again there. Chrome's ⋮ > Settings > Preferences has "Auto-open DevTools for popups" for links that open new windows.
The panels and the questions they answer

head: Question
Chrome panel
Safari tab
This book's drawer
rows: What is in the page right now, and why does it look like that?
What did the code log, and what does this expression return?
Which requests happened, with what status, headers, body and timing?
Network (method, URL, status, type, size, time, headers, body)
Which line is running, and what are the variables?
What does the site store about me?
Why is it slow or janky?

blocks.text: Press [[Esc]] in Chrome DevTools to open the **drawer** under any panel: a Console you can use while you look at Elements or Sources, plus extra tools (Network conditions, Changes, Rendering). Safari has a split console at the bottom of every tab.
The Console is a REPL for the page

The Console is a read-eval-print loop running **inside the page**. What you type is evaluated in the page's global scope, with access to its variables, its DOM and its network, exactly as if it were one more script. That makes it three things at once: a log viewer, a calculator for JavaScript, and a remote control for the page.

items.text: Type an expression and press [[Return]]: the result appears after `<` (Chrome) or as an output line. Statements such as `let x = 1` print `undefined`, because a declaration has no value.
[[⇧Return]] adds a new line without running, for multi-line code. ↑ and ↓ walk your history. [[Tab]] or → accepts autocompletion.

Chrome **eagerly evaluates** expressions without side effects as you type and shows the result in grey underneath. It refuses to preview anything that could change state, so `items.push(1)` waits for Return.
Top-level `await` works: `await fetch('/api/status').then((r) => r.json())`.
Chrome lets you re-declare `let` and `const` in the Console (scripts cannot), so you can re-run a snippet after editing it. This book's drawer allows it too.

Objects print as live, expandable trees. Expanding one later shows its properties **as they are now**, not when logged; Chrome marks this with a small "i" icon. Log `structuredClone(obj)` or `JSON.stringify(obj)` when you need a snapshot.
[[⌘K]] (or `clear()`) clears the Console.

blocks.text: Levels, filters and context

Every message has a **level**: verbose (`console.debug`), info (`log`, `info`), warning and error. The level dropdown hides whole levels; `debug` messages are hidden by default in Chrome until you tick **Verbose**. The filter box keeps matching lines: plain text, a regular expression such as `/5\d\d/`, `-text` to hide lines, and `url:app.js` to keep messages from one file. Errors include a link (`app.js:12`) that opens the line in Sources.

Two settings save time. **Preserve log** (Console settings, the gear) keeps messages across page loads, which you need when a form submission or a redirect navigates away from the page that logged the error. The **JavaScript context** dropdown (labelled `top`) chooses which frame the Console evaluates in: a page that embeds iframes, such as this book, has one context per frame, and `$('h1')` searches only the selected one.
The Console API

`console` is an object available to every script, in browsers and in Node. Its methods write to the Console at different levels and in different shapes. The first argument can contain **format specifiers**, which consume the following arguments in order:

head: Specifier
Formats the next argument as
Example
rows: an expandable object (DOM elements as nodes or as objects)
CSS for the text that follows (browsers only; Node and this book's runner ignore it)

tokens.exp: the method; console.warn, error, info and debug take the same arguments at other levels
the format string; each specifier consumes the next argument in order
any argument left over is appended after a space, inspected if it is an object
one call prints one line (or one expandable entry in a browser)

blocks.out:
6 devices, 5 online, first is router
scan finished
nas did not answer
backup job failed
[OK] pi answered

blocks.text: In a real browser the warning has a yellow background, the error a red one with a stack you can expand, and `[OK]` is green and bold. The text is the same everywhere, which is why this book can check it.
Tables, groups, counters and assertions

blocks.text: `console.count(label)` keeps one counter per label, so it answers "how often does this line run, and for which values?" without any variables of your own. `console.assert` prints only when its condition is false, which makes it a cheap tripwire you can leave in development code. The first assertion passed and printed nothing.

`console.log` prints nested objects only to a limited depth. `console.dir` takes an options object in Node (`depth`), and in browsers shows a DOM element as a JavaScript object with all its properties instead of as HTML:

blocks.name: console.log()
blocks.sum: Print values to the console, optionally through a format string with %s, %d, %f, %o and %c specifiers.

how.text: Each argument is converted for display: strings print raw at the top level, other values as an inspectable representation (expandable trees in browsers, `util.inspect` text in Node). Arguments are separated by spaces. When the first argument is a string containing `%`, specifiers are replaced by the following arguments and the rest are appended.

`console.info`, `console.warn`, `console.error` and `console.debug` take the same arguments and differ only in level: the Console colours and filters by level, and Node writes `warn` and `error` to stderr instead of stdout.

examples.desc: Format a status line from fetched data
examples.code:
const s = await (await fetch('/api/status')).json();
console.log('%s: %d of %d devices online, load %f', s.host, s.online, s.devices, s.load[0]);

examples.desc: Log only the offline devices from a fetch chain
examples.code: fetch('/api/devices').then((r) => r.json()).then((list) => list.filter((d) => !d.online).forEach((d) => console.log('%s is offline (%s)', d.name, d.ip)));

gotchas: A logged object is shown live in browsers: expanding it later shows its current state. Log a copy (`structuredClone(obj)`) or `JSON.stringify(obj)` when the value changes afterwards.

blocks.name: console.table()
blocks.sum: Show an array of objects (or an object of objects) as a table with one row per item and one column per property.

how.text: Rows are the array indexes or object keys; columns are the union of the properties found in the rows. Primitive items get a single `Values` column. The second argument limits and orders the columns. Browsers render a sortable grid (click a header); Node draws a box table with Unicode lines.
It is the fastest way to eyeball API data: one call turns a JSON array into something you can scan for the odd value out.

examples.desc: Two columns of the device inventory
Fetch, filter and tabulate in one chain

blocks.name: console.dir()
blocks.sum: Print a value as an inspectable object; in browsers, show DOM elements as objects instead of HTML.

how.text: `console.log(el)` shows an element as its HTML; `console.dir(el)` shows it as a JavaScript object, so you can browse properties such as `dataset`, `classList`, `offsetWidth` or `onclick`. In Node the options object sets `depth` (default 2, `null` for unlimited), `colors` and `showHidden`.

examples.desc: Control how deep a nested object is printed
Inspect the first table row on a page as an object, then list its cells

blocks.name: console.group()
blocks.sum: Indent the messages that follow under a label until console.groupEnd(); groups nest.

how.text: Each `group` call prints its label and increases the indentation level for later output; `groupEnd` decreases it. Browsers show groups as collapsible sections, and `groupCollapsed` starts them closed, which keeps verbose per-item logs out of the way until you want them.

examples.desc: One group per device
Group the log lines of each request in a sequence of fetches
examples.code: for (const url of ['/api/status', '/api/devices/9']) { const r = await fetch(url); console.group(url); console.log(r.status, r.statusText); console.groupEnd(); }

gotchas: Forgetting a `groupEnd()` (for example on an early `return`) indents every later message. Close groups in a `finally` block when the code can throw.

blocks.name: console.count()
blocks.sum: Print how many times this label has been counted so far.

how.text: The console keeps a counter per label string and prints `label: N` on each call. Put it inside a function, an event listener or a loop to learn how often it runs and with which values, without adding variables to the code.

examples.desc: Count devices by type
Count every click on the page by element tag (paste into the Console, then click around)

blocks.name: console.time()
blocks.sum: Start a named timer; console.timeLog() prints the elapsed time, console.timeEnd() prints it and stops the timer.

how.text: The timer uses a high-resolution monotonic clock (like `performance.now()`), so it is not affected by changes to the system time. Output looks like `fetch: 41.27ms`. Times include everything that happened in between, other tasks too, so measure several runs and look at the spread, not one number.

examples.desc: Time a request from the Console
Time several requests in parallel and log each as it lands
examples.code: console.time('all'); await Promise.all(['/api/status', '/api/devices'].map((u) => fetch(u).then(() => console.timeLog('all', u)))); console.timeEnd('all');

gotchas: Calling `timeEnd` with a label that was never started prints a warning, not a time. Labels are matched exactly, including case.

blocks.name: console.assert()
blocks.sum: Print an error-level message only when a condition is false.

how.text: When `condition` is truthy nothing happens. When it is falsy the console prints `Assertion failed:` followed by the formatted message, at error level in browsers (with a stack trace you can expand). Unlike Python's `assert` statement it never throws, so execution continues.

examples.desc: A tripwire for bad data
examples.code:
const ports = [22, 80, 70000];
console.assert(ports.every((p) => p > 0 && p < 65536), 'invalid port in %o', ports);

examples.desc: Check every device record from the API has an IPv4 address
examples.code: fetch('/api/devices').then((r) => r.json()).then((list) => list.forEach((d) => console.assert(/^\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/.test(d.ip), 'bad ip on %s', d.name)));

blocks.name: console.trace()
blocks.sum: Print a message together with the current call stack: which functions called this line.

how.text: The output starts with `Trace:` (or `console.trace` in Chrome) and lists each active function with its file and line, innermost first. It answers "who called this?" when a function runs from more places than you expected, without pausing the page.

examples.desc: Find out which code path re-renders the list
Trace every write to a property you suspect is being clobbered
examples.code: (() => { let v = window.theme; Object.defineProperty(window, 'theme', { get: () => v, set: (x) => { console.trace('theme =', x); v = x; } }); })();

gotchas: Stack traces differ between browsers and builds, and minified code shows minified names unless source maps are loaded.

blocks.text: Console utilities: shortcuts that only exist in the Console

DevTools adds a set of helpers to the Console's scope. They are **not** part of JavaScript: a page script that calls `$$()` fails with a `ReferenceError` (unless the page defines its own `$`, as jQuery did, in which case the page's version wins).

Does
Chrome
Safari
This drawer
rows: the value of the last evaluated expression
array of nodes matching an XPath
put a string, or an object as JSON, on the clipboard
every live object made by a constructor
an expression re-evaluated continuously, pinned at the top

blocks.text: Drill: scrape a router status page
This practice page imitates a home router's admin page. Do each step in its **Console** and predict the result first.

blocks.code:
gw-01 firmware 3.0.4

WAN: connected · 203.0.113.42 · uptime 3 d 1 h

DHCP clients (4)
NameIPMACLink
macbook192.168.1.23f0:18:98:3a:6d:215 GHz
pi192.168.1.50dc:a6:32:4f:10:50wired
printer192.168.1.703c:2a:f4:12:34:702.4 GHz

items.text: Count the client rows: `$$('#clients tbody tr').length`.
List the IPs: `$$('#clients td:nth-child(2)').map((td) => td.textContent)`. `$$` returns an array, so `map` works directly; `document.querySelectorAll` would need `[...]` first.
Build records: `rows = $$('#clients tbody tr').map((tr) => { const [name, ip, mac, link] = [...tr.cells].map((c) => c.textContent); return { name, ip, mac, link }; })`, then `console.table(rows)`.
Copy them out: `copy(rows)`. In Terminal, `pbpaste | python3 -m json.tool` pretty-prints what you scraped, and `pbpaste > ~/lab/clients.json` saves it for the Python chapters' tools.
XPath works too: `$x('//tr[td[4]="wired"]/td[1]').map((td) => td.textContent)` returns the wired clients.
Change the page: `$('h1').textContent = 'gw-01 (edited from the Console)'`. Press **Reload page** and it is back: you changed the DOM in memory, not the file on the server.
Select the `table` in **Elements**, then return to Console and type `$0.rows.length` (5: one header row plus four body rows).

blocks.sum: The element currently selected in the Elements panel, available in the Console.

how.text: Selecting a node in Elements, or with the element picker (⇧⌘C), assigns it to `$0`. This bridges the two panels: find an element visually, then script it. In Chrome `$1` to `$4` hold the four previous selections; in Safari `$1` and up are earlier Console results instead.

examples.desc: Ask the selected element about itself
Collect the text of every child of the selected list

blocks.name: $() and $$()
blocks.sum: Console shorthands for querySelector() and for querySelectorAll() returned as an array.

how.text: `$` returns the first match or `null`; `$$` returns an `Array` (not a NodeList), so `map`, `filter` and `reduce` chain straight onto it. The optional second argument limits the search to a subtree. If the page defines its own global `$` (jQuery, for example), the page's function shadows the Console's.

examples.desc: Every link on the page that leaves your LAN
Scrape a table into records and copy them as JSON
examples.code: copy($$('#clients tbody tr').map((tr) => Object.fromEntries([...tr.cells].map((c, i) => [['name', 'ip', 'mac', 'link'][i], c.textContent]))));

gotchas: These helpers exist only in the Console. Code in your page must use `document.querySelector` and `document.querySelectorAll`.

blocks.name: $x()
blocks.sum: Evaluate an XPath expression against the page and return the matching nodes as an array.

how.text: It wraps `document.evaluate` with an ordered snapshot result. XPath can do what CSS selectors cannot: match on text content (`//td[.="wired"]`), walk up to ancestors (`ancestor::tr`) and select earlier siblings. [XML and friends](#xml) covers XPath in depth.

examples.desc: Rows whose link column says wired
The name of every client on 5 GHz, via its sibling cell

blocks.name: copy()
blocks.sum: Copy a value to the system clipboard: strings as they are, objects and arrays as pretty JSON.

how.text: Objects are serialised with `JSON.stringify` and indentation, DOM elements as their HTML. Combined with `$$` scraping it is the shortest path from a web page to a file or a shell pipeline on your Mac: copy in the browser, `pbpaste` in Terminal.

examples.desc: Copy the page's outgoing links
Copy fetched API data, then validate and save it from Terminal

gotchas: Some sites redefine `copy`; Chrome's helper then loses. `navigator.clipboard.writeText(text)` is the scriptable equivalent and works in page code too (it needs a user gesture or focus).

blocks.name: inspect()
blocks.sum: Reveal an element in the Elements panel (or a function in Sources) and select it as $0.

how.text: The reverse of `$0`: you find something with code, and `inspect` switches to the panel that shows it. Passing a function in Chrome or Safari opens its source.

examples.desc: Jump to the first offline row in Elements
Find the element with the most children and reveal it

blocks.name: monitorEvents()
blocks.sum: Log every event of the given types that fires on an element; unmonitorEvents() stops it.

how.text: DevTools attaches listeners for you and logs each event object as it fires. In Chrome you can pass event types or whole categories (`mouse`, `key`, `touch`, `control`). It is the quickest way to learn which events a widget really fires, and in which order, before you write a listener.

examples.desc: Watch what typing in a search box fires
Monitor the selected element, then list the listeners it already had (Chrome and Safari)

gotchas: Monitoring `window` for `mouse` events floods the Console. Pick specific types and call `unmonitorEvents` when done.

blocks.text: Changing the page live

Because the Console runs inside the page, anything a script can do you can do by hand: rewrite text, add classes, insert CSS rules, call the page's own functions, fetch from its API with its cookies. Three habits make this safe and useful.

**Know what you changed.** Every edit lives in the page's memory. Reloading throws it away and the server's files are untouched, which also means you cannot break a website for anyone else from your Console. To keep an edit across reloads in Chrome, use **Local Overrides** (Sources > Overrides: pick a folder, then edits in Sources or Styles are saved and served in place of the network copy), or map a local folder with **Workspaces** so DevTools edits write straight to your project files.
**Prototype, then port.** Try a CSS fix in Styles or a DOM change in the Console until it looks right, then put the same change in your source file and reload to confirm.
**Play with the page.** `document.designMode = 'on'` makes the whole page editable like a text document; click any text and type. Set it back to `'off'` when done.

pi 192.168.1.50

items.text: Toggle a class: `$('[data-id="3"]').classList.toggle('offline')`.
Inject a rule: `$('#page-css').sheet.insertRule('.card.offline b::after { content: " (down)"; color: #b00020; }')`.

Pull live data into the page: `for (const d of await (await fetch('/api/devices')).json()) $('body').insertAdjacentHTML('beforeend', '
' + d.name + '
')`. Then think about what would happen if a device name contained ``: that is cross-site scripting, and [The DOM](#dom) shows why `textContent` is the safe choice.
Watch the **Network** pane while you run the fetch, and **Elements** as the new nodes appear.

blocks.text: Elements: the live DOM, its styles and its box

The Elements panel shows the **DOM**, the tree the browser built and scripts have since modified, which is often very different from the HTML source (⌥⌘U). The parser repairs bad markup, scripts add and remove nodes, and frameworks render everything at run time; when "view source" and Elements disagree, Elements is what the browser is actually rendering.
What you can do there, in Chrome and Safari alike:

items.text: **Edit**: double-click a tag name, attribute or text to change it; right-click > Edit as HTML (Chrome: [[fn F2]]); drag nodes to reorder; [[Delete]] removes the node; [[H]] toggles `visibility: hidden` on it.

**Copy**: right-click > Copy > Copy selector, Copy JS path or Copy XPath gives you an expression for `$()` or `$x()` in the Console (generated selectors are brittle; shorten them before using them in code).
**Break on changes**: right-click > Break on > subtree modifications, attribute modifications or node removal pauses the script that makes the change (see the debugger section).

**Styles, Computed and box model**: the sidebar explains every pixel, as covered in [CSS](#css/debug-css): winners first, crossed-out losers, warning icons for invalid declarations, `:hov` to force hover and focus states, `.cls` to toggle classes.

**Device mode** (Chrome ⇧⌘M) and **Responsive Design Mode** (Safari ⌃⌘R) resize the viewport to phone and tablet sizes, emulate touch and device pixel ratio, and let you test media queries without resizing the window.

blocks.text: The drawer in this book's playgrounds shows the tree, highlights the element under your mouse in the page, and shows the selected element's box model and key computed values. It cannot edit in place; use the Console with `$0` for that, as in the CSS chapter.
Network: every request, timed
Open the Network panel **before** the page loads (or reload with it open), because it only records while DevTools is open. Each row is one request.

head: Column
Tells you
rows: what was requested; hover for the full URL
`200`, `304`, `404`, `500`, or `(failed)`, `(blocked:...)`, `(canceled)` for requests that never got a response
which file and line, or which other resource, started it; click to jump there
bytes over the wire, or `(memory cache)` / `(disk cache)` when nothing was downloaded
total from start to the last byte
when each request started and how long each phase took, on one shared timeline

blocks.text: The filter bar narrows the list by type (**Fetch/XHR**, Doc, CSS, JS, Img, Media, Font, WS) or by text, and supports properties such as `status-code:404`, `method:POST` and `domain:lab.local`. Three checkboxes matter constantly: **Preserve log** (keep requests across navigations, essential for form posts and redirects), **Disable cache** (while DevTools is open, every request goes to the network, so you always test your latest CSS and JS) and the **throttling** dropdown (No throttling, Fast 4G, Slow 4G, 3G, Offline, or custom profiles).
Click a request for its details:

items.text: **Headers**: the General block (URL, method, status, remote address), the response headers (`Content-Type`, `Cache-Control`, `Set-Cookie`, `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`) and the request headers the browser sent (`Cookie`, `Origin`, `Referer`, `Authorization`).
**Payload**: query string parameters and the request body of a POST, parsed.
**Preview** and **Response**: the body, rendered (JSON as a tree, images shown) or raw.
**Initiator**: the call stack that issued the request.
**Timing**: where the time went.

blocks.text: Reading the timing breakdown
The Timing tab splits one request into phases. They are the same phases you measured with `curl -w` in [HTTP](#http/timing), viewed from inside the browser:

blocks.code:
Queueing / Stalled    waiting for a free connection (browsers allow about 6 per host on HTTP/1.1)
 DNS Lookup            name → address                         curl: time_namelookup
 Initial connection    TCP handshake (and TLS, shown as SSL)  curl: time_connect, time_appconnect
 Request sent          the request bytes leave
 ⟪y:Waiting for server response⟫  server think time: ⟪y:TTFB⟫       curl: time_starttransfer − time_appconnect
 Content Download      the body arrives                       curl: time_total − time_starttransfer

blocks.text: Older Chrome versions label the waiting phase "Waiting (TTFB)". A connection that is reused shows no DNS or connection phase at all. As a rule of thumb: long DNS or connection phases point at the network or a far-away server, a long wait points at the server's code or database, and a long download points at a large response or a slow link. Throttle to Slow 4G and reload to feel what a phone on a weak signal gets.
Replay, export and block

items.text: **Copy as cURL** (right-click the request > Copy > Copy as cURL) gives you a `curl` command with the same method, URL, headers, cookies and body, ready to paste into Terminal, edit and repeat. It is the bridge to everything in the HTTP chapter.
**Copy as fetch** gives the same request as a `fetch()` call; paste it into the Console to replay it from the page, then change a header or the body and run it again.

**Block request URL** or **Block request domain** (right-click) makes the browser fail that request on purpose: the fastest way to test how your page behaves when the API, a font or an analytics script is down.
**Save all as HAR** exports every request with headers and bodies for a bug report. A HAR file contains your cookies and tokens; treat it like a password and redact it before sharing.

blocks.text: Replaying from the Console is also how you learn exactly what a request sends. The practice server's `/api/echo` returns what it received:
Drill: requests that went wrong
This page makes five requests when it loads. Open **Network** (it opens first), let it finish, then click each row and read its status, headers and response before you read on.

blocks.code: Lab status

blocks.text: What you should find: `/api/status` is a clean `200`. `/api/devices/9` is a `404` whose body says `device 9 not found`. The POST is a `422 Unprocessable Content` because `192.168.1.300` is not an IPv4 address; its Payload shows the JSON you sent. `/api/flaky` appears **twice**: a `503` with a `Retry-After: 1` header, then a `200` from the retry loop (a polite client would wait the full second the header asks for). The last request shows a CORS error and the Console prints the browser's explanation: the server answered, but without an `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header the browser refused to let the page read the response. Notice that none of the failed statuses threw an exception in the code; `fetch` only rejects when there is no usable response at all.

blocks.name: Copy as cURL
blocks.sum: Turn any request in the Network panel into a curl command that reproduces it from Terminal.
blocks.syntax: Network panel > right-click a request > Copy > Copy as cURL

how.text: DevTools writes a single-quoted `curl` command with the URL, `-X` for methods other than GET, one `-H` per request header the browser sent (including `Cookie` and `Authorization`), and `--data-raw` with the body. Paste it into Terminal and it behaves like the browser's request, minus the browser's own caching and CORS rules (curl has no origin and ignores CORS entirely).
From there you have the whole HTTP toolkit: add `-i` to see response headers, `-w` for timing, `-o` to save the body, or loop it in a script.

examples.desc: What a copied request looks like (shortened)
examples.code: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/devices.json' -H 'Accept: */*' -H 'Referer: http://127.0.0.1:8000/' -H 'User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 10_15_7) ...'

the browser's identity string, copied verbatim

examples.desc: Replay it quietly and pretty-print the JSON response

gotchas: The copied command contains your session cookies and tokens. Never paste it into a chat, a bug tracker or a shared document without deleting those headers.

blocks.text: Sources and the debugger

`console.log` debugging means guessing where to print, reloading, reading, and guessing again. A debugger pauses the program at a line you choose and shows you **everything**: every variable in scope, the chain of calls that led there, and the ability to run one line at a time. It is the same tool you used in PyCharm in [Errors and debugging](#py-errors/pycharm), built into the browser. This book's drawer has no debugger, so practise in a real browser with this two-file page. Create it in `~/lab/web/debug/` (PyCharm or `nano`):

blocks.code: loading...

blocks.text: Open `http://127.0.0.1:8000/` in Chrome with the Console open. The summary stays at "loading..." and the Console shows the error, which reads differently in each engine:

head: Browser
Message
rows: `Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'online')` with `at countOnline (app.js:12:17)`

blocks.text: Both say the same thing: on line 12, `list[i]` was `undefined`. Now find out *why* instead of guessing:

items.text: Click the `app.js:12` link. Sources opens with the line highlighted.
Click the line number **12** to set a breakpoint (a blue marker), then reload. Execution stops *before* line 12 runs, on every pass through the loop.

Look at **Scope**: `list` is the array, `i` is 0, `online` is 0. Press **Resume** (F8) and it stops again with `i` at 1; press **Step over** (F10 or ⌘') to walk line by line instead. Hover over `list.length` in the code to see `4`.

That is slow for long loops. Right-click the marker > **Edit breakpoint** and make it conditional: `i >= 3`. Reload: it now pauses only when `i` is 3, then 4. At `i = 4`, `list[4]` is `undefined`: the loop runs one step too far because of `<=` on line 11. (A breakpoint on the `for` line itself would pause only once, at `let i = 0`.)
Read the **Call Stack**: `countOnline`, called by `render`, called from the top-level script (the anonymous frame). Click a frame to see that function's variables.
In the Console, while paused, type `list[i]` or `i < list.length`: the Console evaluates **in the paused frame**, with its local variables.
Fix `<=` to `<` in `app.js` in your editor, save, reload: `3 of 4 online`. Remove the breakpoint.

blocks.text: DOM and event breakpoints answer the questions that are hardest otherwise: "which script keeps hiding this element?" (break on attribute modifications of the element) and "what runs when I click this button?" (an event listener breakpoint on click, then step into).
Stepping

head: Action
Chrome keys
What it does
rows: run the current line, including any functions it calls, and stop at the next line
enter the function called on this line
finish the current function and stop in its caller

blocks.text: Safari's Sources tab has the same four buttons above its call stack. The sidebar sections are the same in both browsers: **Scope** (Local, Closure, Script, Global: the closure variables from [JavaScript in Depth](#js-deeper) are visible here), **Watch** (expressions re-evaluated at every pause) and **Call Stack**.
Minified code and source maps

Production JavaScript is usually bundled and minified: one long line, short variable names. Click the `{}` (pretty print) button in Sources to reformat it. Better, build tools emit a **source map**, a JSON file that maps positions in the minified file back to your original files. The bundle ends with a comment like `//# sourceMappingURL=app.min.js.map`; DevTools downloads the map and shows, and lets you set breakpoints in, the original sources. Publishing source maps publishes your source code, so some sites only keep them internally.

blocks.name: debugger
blocks.sum: A statement that pauses execution at that point when a debugger is attached; otherwise it does nothing.

how.text: When DevTools (or Node's inspector, or an editor's debugger) is attached, reaching `debugger;` behaves exactly like a breakpoint on that line: execution stops, and Scope, Watch and Call Stack show the state. With no debugger attached the statement is a no-op, so it is harmless in a page nobody inspects, but it should never be committed.

It is handy where clicking a line number is awkward: code generated at run time, an event handler you cannot find in a large bundle, or a condition that is easier to write in code (`if (d.ip === undefined) debugger;`).

examples.desc: Pause only for the record that breaks things
examples.code: for (const d of devices) { if (!d.ip) debugger; render(d); }

examples.desc: Pause inside a fetch chain to inspect the parsed data before it is used
examples.code: fetch('/api/devices').then((r) => r.json()).then((list) => { debugger; return list.filter((d) => d.online); });

gotchas: Linters such as ESLint flag `debugger` statements (rule `no-debugger`). Remove them before you commit, or use conditional breakpoints, which live in DevTools and never touch the file.

blocks.text: Storage: what the site remembers
Chrome's **Application** panel and Safari's **Storage** tab show everything a site keeps in your browser, per **origin** (scheme + host + port), and let you edit or delete it.

head: Store
Lifetime
Size
Read by
rows: JavaScript on the same origin, synchronously
until the tab closes; each tab has its own
JavaScript on the same origin, in that tab
sent to the server with every matching request; JavaScript too unless `HttpOnly`
JavaScript, asynchronously; a real database for structured data and files

blocks.text: Cookies are the only store the server sees, because the browser attaches them to requests in the `Cookie` header. Their attributes are security controls, shown as columns in the cookie table:

head: Attribute
Effect
rows: JavaScript cannot read or write it (`document.cookie` does not show it); only HTTP requests carry it. Session cookies should have it, so an XSS bug cannot steal them
sent only over HTTPS (localhost is treated as secure for development)
never sent on requests that come from another site
sent on top-level navigations from other sites (clicking a link) but not on their embedded requests or form POSTs; Chrome's default when the attribute is missing
sent everywhere, which requires `Secure`; used for deliberate third-party embeds
which hosts and paths receive it
when it dies; without either it is a session cookie

blocks.code: Theme: · Visits in this session:

blocks.text: In its **Console**:

items.text: `Object.entries(localStorage)` lists every key and value; `localStorage.theme = 'light'` changes one (values are always strings: `localStorage.n = 5` stores `'5'`).
`document.cookie` returns all readable cookies as one string, `name=value; name2=value2`, without their attributes.
`document.cookie = 'lab_tz=; Max-Age=0'` deletes a cookie: writing to `document.cookie` sets **one** cookie, it does not replace them all.

`sessionStorage.clear()` empties session storage. Switch to **Storage** after each command to see the change. This practice page keeps everything in memory, so **Reload page** starts fresh; a real site keeps it on disk.

blocks.text: In a real browser, Chrome's Application > Storage > **Clear site data** wipes every store for the origin at once, the quickest way to test what a first-time visitor sees.

Any script running on the page can read `localStorage`, including an injected one if your site has an XSS bug, and a browser extension with page access. Auth tokens belong in `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite` cookies set by the server. And never put API keys or passwords in client JavaScript at all: anyone can read them in Sources or Network.

blocks.name: document.cookie
blocks.sum: Read all script-visible cookies for the page as one string, or set a single cookie with its attributes.
blocks.syntax: document.cookie -> 'a=1; b=2'      document.cookie = 'name=value; Max-Age=SECONDS; Path=/; SameSite=Lax; Secure'

how.text: Reading returns `name=value` pairs joined by `; `, without attributes and without `HttpOnly` cookies. Assigning parses one cookie string and stores or updates that single cookie; the attributes after the first `;` control its scope and lifetime. Values should be URL-encoded (`encodeURIComponent`) because `;`, `,` and spaces are special.
The server sets cookies with `Set-Cookie` response headers, which you can read in the Network panel; DevTools' cookie table shows all of them, `HttpOnly` included, with every attribute.

examples.desc: Set a one-year preference cookie
Turn the cookie string into an object you can query

gotchas: To delete a cookie you must set it again with `Max-Age=0` and the same `Path` and `Domain` it was created with; otherwise you create a second cookie instead.

blocks.text: Performance and Lighthouse

JavaScript in a page runs on one **main thread**, which also handles input, style, layout and paint. Any task that holds it longer than **50 ms** is a **long task**: clicks and keypresses wait behind it and the page feels stuck. Chrome's **Performance** panel (Safari: **Timelines**) records everything the main thread does:

items.text: Open Performance, click Record (●) or the reload-and-record button, use the page, stop.

Read the **Main** track as a flame chart: wide bars are slow, the bars below a call are what it called. Long tasks get a red corner; a purple **Layout** bar marked "Forced reflow" means script made the browser compute layout synchronously.
Click a bar to see its source file and line, and jump to Sources.
Use the CPU throttling option (4× or 6× slowdown) so your fast Mac behaves like a mid-range phone.

blocks.text: The classic self-inflicted slowdown is **layout thrashing**: reading a layout value (`offsetWidth`, `getBoundingClientRect()`, `getComputedStyle`) right after writing a style forces the browser to recompute layout immediately, and doing that in a loop recomputes it on every iteration:
To see a long task on purpose, paste this into the Console of any page while Performance is recording; the page cannot respond to clicks for 300 ms:

blocks.code:
const t0 = performance.now();
while (performance.now() - t0 < 300) { /* busy: the main thread is blocked */ }

blocks.text: **Lighthouse** (Chrome) audits a page and scores four categories from 0 to 100: Performance, Accessibility, Best Practices and SEO. Run it in a Guest or Incognito window so extensions do not skew the result, and run it more than once, because performance scores vary between runs. The performance part reports the **Core Web Vitals**, the metrics Google uses for real-user experience: **LCP** (Largest Contentful Paint, good at 2.5 s or less), **INP** (Interaction to Next Paint, good at 200 ms or less; it replaced FID in 2024) and **CLS** (Cumulative Layout Shift, good at 0.1 or less). Treat the score as a to-do list sorted by impact, not as a grade; the accessibility audit alone catches missing labels, low contrast and missing `alt` text that you would otherwise ship. Safari's **Audit** tab runs a similar set of accessibility checks.
A debugging recipe
Most front-end bugs fall to the same loop. Do the steps in order and resist jumping to a fix before step 4.

items.text: **Reproduce** reliably. Note the exact steps; turn on Preserve log if the bug involves navigation.

**Read the error** completely: the type (`TypeError`, `ReferenceError`, `SyntaxError`), the message, and the file and line. Click the link. `Cannot read properties of null` almost always means a selector found nothing; `x is not a function` means `x` holds something else than you think; `Unexpected token '<'` from `res.json()` means the server sent HTML (an error page) where you expected JSON.
**Check the network** for anything data-driven: right URL? status? Does the response body contain what the code expects?
**Pause and look.** A breakpoint just before the failing line shows the actual values. Compare them with what you assumed.
**Form one hypothesis** that explains everything you saw. Test it in the Console while paused.
**Fix it in your source file**, not in DevTools.
**Confirm** with the same steps. If it still fails, your hypothesis was wrong; go back to 4 with what you learned.

blocks.text: The playground below contains four bugs. Use the recipe on it: the Console shows the first error, **Network** shows what the code fetched, and **Elements** shows what was rendered. The Practice section asks you to fix the same code with an automatic check.

blocks.code:
loading...

    --- css li.offline { color: #b00020; } --- js async function main() { const res = await fetch('/api/device'); const devices = res.json(); const list = document.querySelector('#device-list'); let online = 0; for (const d of devices) { const li = document.createElement('li'); li.textContent = `${d.name} ${d.ip}`; if (d.Online = false) li.classList.add('offline'); else online++; list.append(li); } document.querySelector('#summary').textContent = `${online} of ${devices.length} online`; } main();

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items.text: **Opening DevTools after the request.** Network records only while it is open. Open it, then reload.
**Testing stale files.** Tick **Disable cache** while developing, or hard-reload (Chrome ⇧⌘R, Safari ⌥⌘R).
**Fixing in DevTools and forgetting the file.** Styles and Console edits vanish on reload. Port them to the source (Chrome's Changes drawer lists them).
**Using `$` or `$$` in page code.** They are Console helpers. Scripts need `document.querySelector()` and `querySelectorAll()`.
**Reading an expanded object as a snapshot.** Browsers show the object's current state when you expand it. Log `JSON.stringify(obj)` for a snapshot.
**Evaluating in the wrong frame.** On a page with iframes, check the context dropdown (`top`) before concluding that an element does not exist.
**Treating `fetch` errors as exceptions.** A `404` or `500` resolves normally with `res.ok === false`. Check the status; the Network pane shows it.
**Sharing a HAR file or a copied cURL command unredacted.** Both contain cookies and tokens.
**Leaving `debugger;` and noisy `console.log` calls in committed code.** Use logpoints and conditional breakpoints, which live in DevTools.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Scrape the client table to JSON

task.text: The page is the router status page from the drill. Print the DHCP clients as **one line of JSON**: an array of objects with the keys `name`, `ip`, `mac` and `link`, in table order. This practice frame provides `$$()` like the Console does (in your own page scripts you would use `document.querySelectorAll`). In a real browser you would finish with `copy(rows)` instead of printing.

hints: `tr.cells` is the row's list of `td` elements; spread it with `[...tr.cells]` to use `map`.
Destructure the four texts: `const [name, ip, mac, link] = [...tr.cells].map((td) => td.textContent);` then return `{ name, ip, mac, link }`.

why.text: `$$` returns a real array, so the whole scrape is one `map`: rows to cells, cells to text, text to an object. `JSON.stringify` turns the result into text another program can read, and `copy()` puts that text on the clipboard so `pbpaste | python3 -m json.tool` can take over in Terminal. Selecting `tbody tr` instead of `tr` keeps the header row out.

blocks.title: Debugging hunt: four bugs, one page

task.text: This is the code from the Debugging hunt playground. When it works, the list shows all six devices, `nas` has the class `offline`, and the summary reads `5 of 6 online`. Fix the four bugs. Follow the recipe: run it, read the error, fix only what that error explains, run again. The playground version above lets you watch the Network pane for the request.

hints: The first error is `devices is not iterable`. What does `res.json()` return, and what must you do with it?
After that fix the same error comes back. Log `devices`, or look at the request's status in Network: the URL is wrong (the API is `/api/devices`).
`Cannot read properties of null (reading 'append')` means `querySelector` found nothing. Compare the selector with the `id` in the page.
The last bug is on the `if` line: one `=` assigns instead of comparing, and property names are case-sensitive (`online`).

why.text: Each bug produces a different symptom. A missing `await` leaves a Promise where data was expected. A wrong URL returns a `404` with an error object, which `fetch` does **not** treat as a failure, so only the Network pane or a status check reveals it. A wrong selector returns `null`, which fails one line later. And `d.Online = false` is an assignment that evaluates to `false`, so the branch never runs and nothing is ever marked offline, a bug with no error message at all. Reading the actual values (Console, Network, breakpoints) finds all four faster than rereading the code.

blocks.title: Read the Network pane

task.text: Open the "Requests to read" practice page in the Network section and answer from the panel alone, without reading the page's code: (1) Which requests returned a 4xx or 5xx status, and what does each response body say? (2) Which request never produced a readable response, and what does the Console say about it? (3) `/api/flaky` appears twice. What header in the first response tells a client what to do, and what did the code do?

hints: Click each row; the Headers section shows the status and response headers, the Response section shows the body. Look at the Status column colours first.
blocks.solution:
(1) GET /api/devices/9: 404, {"error":"device 9 not found"}. POST /api/devices: 422, {"error":"ip is not an IPv4 address"} (the Payload shows ip 192.168.1.300). GET /api/flaky: 503, {"error":"try again"}.
(2) The request to https://nocors.example/api/status: the browser blocked the response because it lacked Access-Control-Allow-Origin; the Console shows a CORS policy error and the code caught TypeError: Failed to fetch.
(3) Retry-After: 1 asks the client to wait a second before retrying. The code waited 300 ms and retried; the second attempt returned 200 {"ok":true,"attempt":2}.

why.text: Status codes, response bodies and headers are the server's side of the story; the Console is the browser's. A CORS failure is the one case where the server did answer but the page is not allowed to see it, so it shows up as a failed request plus a Console error. Reading these before touching the code tells you whether the bug is in the client, the server or the contract between them.

blocks.title: Copy as cURL against your own server

task.text: Serve `~/lab/web/debug/` (the two files from the debugger section) with Python on port 8000. Open it in Chrome with the Network panel open, right-click the `app.js` request, and choose Copy > Copy as cURL. Paste it into a second Terminal tab and run it. Then edit the command so it only prints the status code, the content type and the size, and finally replay it with an `If-Modified-Since` header to get a `304`.

hints: `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{content_type} %{size_download}\n' URL` prints just those three values.
Get the date the server sends with `curl -sI URL | grep -i last-modified`, then pass it back with `-H 'If-Modified-Since: ...'`.
blocks.solution:
cd ~/lab/web/debug && python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1
# second tab: paste the copied command, then trim it to:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{content_type} %{size_download}\n' 'http://127.0.0.1:8000/app.js' -H 'Accept: */*'
lm=$(curl -sI http://127.0.0.1:8000/app.js | awk -F': ' 'tolower($1)=="last-modified" {print $2}' | tr -d '\r')
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -H "If-Modified-Since: $lm" http://127.0.0.1:8000/app.js

why.text: The copied command reproduces the browser's request header for header, and every Python log line it causes looks like the browser's. Trimming it shows which headers matter. The `304` is the same revalidation the browser performs when its cache holds a copy: the server compares the date with the file's modification time and sends no body when nothing changed. Expect `200 text/javascript` and the file's size in bytes; older Python versions label `.js` files `application/javascript`.

blocks.verify: curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:8000/app.js | grep -q '^200$' && echo "OK: server answers 200 for app.js"

blocks.title: Break it, then make it survive: retry /api/flaky

task.text: The starter fetches `/api/flaky` once. Run it: the first call to that endpoint always fails with `503`, so the program gives up. Make it **retry up to 3 attempts**, stopping at the first success. For each attempt, open a `console.group('attempt N')`, log `status <code>` inside it, and close the group. After a success, print the JSON body with `JSON.stringify`. (Wrap the code in an `async function main()` as in the starter; exercises run as classic scripts.)

hints: A `for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= 3; attempt++)` loop around the fetch; `if (res.ok) { ...; return; }` ends it early.
Put `console.groupEnd()` before the `return` as well, or use `try { ... } finally { console.groupEnd(); }` so every group is closed.

why.text: `fetch` resolves for a `503`, so the retry decision is yours: check `res.ok` (status 200 to 299). Groups make each attempt's lines visibly belong together in the Console, and the `finally` block guarantees `groupEnd` runs even when you `return` from inside the `try`. A production retry would also wait between attempts, honouring the `Retry-After` header, and would only retry methods that are safe to repeat; [JavaScript in Depth](#js-deeper) builds a reusable `retry()` helper.

questions.q: In the Chrome Console, what does `$0` refer to?

options.text: The result of the last expression you evaluated
The element currently selected in the Elements panel
The first element on the page

questions.why: Selecting a node in Elements assigns it to `$0` (and the previous ones to `$1`-`$4`). The last result is `$_`.

questions.q: In the Network Timing tab, which phase mostly measures the server's own processing time?
questions.why: Waiting for server response runs from the request being sent to the first byte of the response: the server's think time plus one round trip. curl calls the end point time_starttransfer.

questions.q: A loop over 500 devices misbehaves only for devices that are offline. What is the most efficient way to stop exactly there?

options.text: A line breakpoint, then press Resume until you reach one
A conditional breakpoint with the expression `d.online === false`
An event listener breakpoint on click

questions.why: A conditional breakpoint pauses only when its expression is truthy, so you land on the interesting iterations without editing the code.

questions.q: Can JavaScript running on the page read a cookie that was set with `HttpOnly`?

options.text: No; it is sent with HTTP requests but hidden from scripts

questions.why: `HttpOnly` keeps a cookie out of `document.cookie` entirely, so an XSS bug cannot steal a session cookie protected this way. DevTools still shows it in the cookie table.

questions.q: You fixed a layout in the Styles pane, reloaded, and the fix is gone. Why?

options.text: The browser cached the old CSS
DevTools edits live only in the page's memory; the file on the server never changed

questions.why: Copy the change into your source file, or use Local Overrides or Workspaces to make Chrome save edits to disk.

questions.q: Which JavaScript statement pauses execution at that point when DevTools is open?
questions.why: `debugger;` acts as a breakpoint when a debugger is attached and does nothing otherwise. Remove it before committing.

Next: [The DOM](#dom) turns these Console experiments into code: selecting, creating and changing elements, handling events with delegation, and rendering lists from the practice API safely.

terms.def: The developer tools built into a browser: Elements, Console, Sources, Network, storage and performance panels (Web Inspector in Safari)
Read-eval-print loop: an interactive prompt that evaluates each input and prints the result, like the Console or Python's >>>
Helpers such as $0, $$(), $x() and copy() that exist only in the DevTools Console, not in page scripts
A marker that pauses execution when a line, condition, DOM change, request or event is reached
A breakpoint that logs a message instead of pausing, so you can add logging without editing the file
The chain of active function calls that led to the current line, innermost first
The variables visible at a point in the code: local, closure, script and global
A file that maps minified or compiled code back to the original sources for debugging
The Network panel's timeline showing when each request started and how long each phase took
Time to first byte: the wait between sending a request and receiving the first byte of the response
HTTP Archive: a JSON export of every request and response in a Network recording, including cookies
Any main-thread task longer than 50 ms, during which the page cannot respond to input
Repeatedly forcing synchronous layout by reading layout values right after writing styles
A cookie attribute that hides the cookie from JavaScript while still sending it with requests
A cookie attribute (Strict, Lax, None) that controls whether the cookie is sent on requests from other sites
